title: Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet

learn.hook: Some heroes don't wear capes. They hold a needle, a sitar or a paintbrush — and they never give up.
points: 'Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet' tells the real-life story of Ila Sachani, who creates beautiful embroidery using her feet.
A biography is the true story of a person's life written by someone else, in the third person (he, she, they).
An autobiography is a person's life story written by that person, in the first person (I, me, my).
Life stories are usually told in time order (chronological order) and in the past tense.
Embroidery words: needle, thread, stitch, fabric (cloth), pattern, design.

example.q: Read: (An original life story.) Kiran was born in a small town and lost her sight when she was seven. At first she felt afraid of the dark world around her. Then a teacher taught her Braille, and books opened up again. She practised the sitar for hours every day. At twenty-five, she gave her first concert, and today she teaches music to children who are blind. Put the main events of Kiran's life in order and say what makes her story inspiring.
steps: Lost her sight at seven and felt afraid.
Learnt Braille and could read again.
Practised the sitar every day.
Gave her first concert at twenty-five.
Now teaches music to blind children.
example.answer: Events in order: loses sight → learns Braille → practises sitar → first concert → teaches others. It is inspiring because she overcame fear through hard work and now helps others.

learn.reallife: School libraries often have biographies of scientists, athletes and artists — real people whose lives inspire us.

games.title: Kiran's life in order
games.prompt: Arrange the events in time order
items: Kiran loses her sight at seven.
She learns Braille from a teacher.
She practises the sitar every day.
She gives her first concert at twenty-five.
She teaches music to blind children.

games.title: Biography or autobiography?
items: "She was born in a small village in 1990."
"I was born in a small village in 1990."
"His first invention was a toy car."
"My first invention was a toy car."
written about a person by someone else
written by the person about their own life

quiz.q: In the life story, when did Kiran lose her sight?
quiz.explain: The passage says she lost her sight when she was seven.
steps: The passage gives the age when Kiran lost her sight.
It says she lost it when she was seven.
Other ages in the passage refer to other events.
Answer: when she was seven
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the ages in the passage

quiz.q: How did Kiran feel at first after losing her sight?
quiz.explain: She 'felt afraid of the dark world around her'.
steps: Look for a feeling word right after she lost her sight.
She 'felt afraid of the dark world around her'.
So at first she felt afraid.
Answer: afraid
quiz.mistake: Does not find the feeling word in the passage

quiz.q: In the passage, what helped books 'open up again' for Kiran?
quiz.explain: A teacher taught her Braille, so she could read again.
steps: A teacher taught Kiran Braille.
With Braille she could read again, so books opened up.
Music and concerts came later.
Answer: learning Braille
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of events

quiz.q: What is Braille?
options: a system of raised dots that blind people read by touch
a kind of sign language with hands
quiz.explain: Braille uses patterns of raised dots felt with the fingertips. It was invented by Louis Braille.
steps: Braille is a reading system for people who are blind.
It uses patterns of raised dots felt with the fingertips.
It is not sign language, an instrument or a stitch.
Answer: a system of raised dots that blind people read by touch

quiz.q: What does Kiran do today?
options: She teaches music to children who are blind
quiz.explain: The last line says she teaches music to children who are blind.
steps: The last line tells what Kiran does today.
She teaches music to children who are blind.
She has not stopped music.
Answer: She teaches music to children who are blind

quiz.q: A biography is:
options: a story written by a person about their own life
a life story of a person written by someone else
quiz.explain: 'Bio' means life and 'graphy' means writing; a biography is written by another person.
steps: 'Bio' means life and 'graphy' means writing.
A biography is a life story written by someone else.
A story you write about your own life is an autobiography.
Answer: a life story of a person written by someone else

quiz.q: Which sentence comes from an autobiography?
options: She learnt embroidery from her grandmother.
I learnt embroidery from my grandmother.
He learnt embroidery from his grandmother.
They learnt embroidery from their grandmother.
quiz.explain: Autobiographies use the first person: I, my.
steps: An autobiography is written by the person about their own life.
So it uses the first person: I, my.
'I learnt embroidery from my grandmother' uses I and my.
Answer: I learnt embroidery from my grandmother.

quiz.q: In which order are life stories usually told?
quiz.explain: Life stories usually go from early life to later life.
steps: Life stories go from early life to later life.
That is time order, also called chronological order.
They are not alphabetical or random.
Answer: time order (chronological order)
quiz.mistake: Does not know what chronological means

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I'm reading a book about a real person's life. Is it a story or something else?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A biography is the true story of a real person's life. Inspiring stories make me want to fly higher!
teach.nudge: Is a biography about an imaginary person or a real one?

revise.summary: 'Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet' tells the real-life story of Ila Sachani, who creates beautiful embroidery using her feet. Life stories can be biographies or autobiographies and are usually told in time order.
focus: Putting events of a life story in order
remember: A biography is the true story of a person's life written by someone else, in the third person.
An autobiography is a person's life story written by that person, in the first person.
Life stories are usually told in chronological (time) order and in the past tense.
Braille is a system of raised dots that blind people read by touch.
traps: Don't confuse biography with autobiography: 'I learnt...' belongs to an autobiography.
Don't mix up the ages and order of events in the passage.

learn.hook: What matters more — what you cannot do, or what you choose to do with what you can?
points: A disability is a condition that makes some activities, like seeing, hearing, walking or using one's hands, harder in the usual way. People with disabilities find their own ways and tools to do things.
Use respectful words: 'a person with a disability', 'a wheelchair user', 'a person who is blind'. In India, the word 'Divyang' is also used officially.
Determination means a firm decision to achieve something, however hard it is.
Accessibility means making places and things usable by everyone: ramps, lifts, Braille signs, audio books and Indian Sign Language.
Indian para-athletes such as Avani Lekhara (shooting) have won gold medals at the Paralympic Games.

example.q: Think it through: A new classmate uses a wheelchair, and the class library is up a flight of stairs. What could the class do, and which values does this show?
steps: The problem is access, not the classmate.
Ask the school to use a ramp, a lift or a ground-floor library corner.
Ask the classmate what would help — and include them.
example.answer: Request a ramp or move books to the ground floor and include the classmate; this shows empathy, respect and fairness.

learn.reallife: Ramps at railway stations, Braille on lift buttons and sign-language windows on TV news are accessibility in action.

games.title: Respect and accessibility
items: 'A person with a disability' is a respectful phrase.
It puts the person first.
A ramp helps wheelchair users enter a building.
Ramps replace steps for wheels.
People with disabilities cannot achieve great things.
Many, like Paralympic champions, achieve great things.
Braille signs help people who are blind.
They can read the raised dots by touch.
It is kind to make fun of how someone walks.
Teasing is hurtful; respect everyone.

games.title: Word and meaning
pairs: easy for everyone to use or reach
a sloping path instead of steps
to fill someone with the wish to do something

quiz.q: Which is the most respectful way to describe someone?
options: a person who uses a wheelchair
quiz.explain: Respectful language puts the person first and avoids hurtful words.
steps: Respectful language puts the person first.
It avoids hurtful words like 'case', 'handicapped' or 'thing'.
So: a person who uses a wheelchair.
Answer: a person who uses a wheelchair
quiz.mistake: Does not know which words are hurtful

quiz.q: What does 'determination' mean?
options: a firm decision to achieve something, even if it is hard
quiz.explain: Determination keeps a person going through difficulties.
steps: Determination is a firm decision to achieve something.
It keeps a person going even when it is hard.
It is not luck or anger.
Answer: a firm decision to achieve something, even if it is hard

quiz.q: Which of these makes a building accessible to wheelchair users?
quiz.explain: Ramps let wheelchairs move in and out easily.
steps: Wheelchairs cannot go up steps or stairs.
A ramp lets them move in and out easily.
So a ramp makes a building accessible.
Answer: a ramp
quiz.mistake: Does not think about wheelchair access

quiz.q: Avani Lekhara has won Paralympic gold medals in which sport?
quiz.explain: Avani Lekhara is a para-shooter who has won Paralympic gold.
steps: Avani Lekhara is a para-athlete.
She has won Paralympic gold in shooting.
She is a para-shooter, not a swimmer or cricketer.
Answer: shooting

quiz.q: What is an 'obstacle'?
quiz.explain: An obstacle is anything that stands in the way of progress.
steps: An obstacle stands in the way.
It is something that blocks your way or progress.
It is not a prize or a friend.
Answer: something that blocks your way

quiz.q: 'Ila Sachani creates embroidery using her feet.' What quality does this most show?
quiz.explain: Finding her own way to create art shows great determination.
steps: Ila found her own way to create embroidery, using her feet.
Working hard despite difficulty shows a firm will.
So it shows determination.
Answer: determination
quiz.mistake: Does not connect effort with determination

quiz.q: What does 'inspire' mean?
options: to fill someone with the wish to do something
quiz.explain: An inspiring story makes others want to try hard too.
steps: An inspiring story makes others want to try hard too.
To inspire is to fill someone with the wish to do something.
It is not about breathing out or frightening.
Answer: to fill someone with the wish to do something

quiz.q: A new student is deaf. What would be thoughtful?
options: Face her when you speak and learn a few signs in Indian Sign Language
Shout very loudly in her ear
Talk about her behind her back
quiz.explain: Facing her helps lip-reading, and learning signs helps you communicate.
steps: A deaf student may lip-read and use sign language.
Facing her and learning a few signs in Indian Sign Language helps.
Shouting, ignoring or gossiping are unkind and unhelpful.
Answer: Face her when you speak and learn a few signs in Indian Sign Language
quiz.mistake: Thinks shouting helps people who are deaf

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'If someone cannot use their hands, how can they make art? And what should I say to them?'
teach.praise: Tweet! With determination, people find their own way to do amazing things — and we should always speak with respect!
teach.nudge: How can we speak about people with disabilities in a respectful way?

revise.summary: A disability makes some activities harder in the usual way, and people with disabilities find their own ways and tools to do things. Respectful words, determination and accessibility help everyone take part.
focus: Meaning of determination, obstacle and inspire
remember: Use respectful words: 'a person with a disability', 'a wheelchair user', 'a person who is blind'; 'Divyang' is also used officially.
Determination means a firm decision to achieve something, however hard it is.
Accessibility means making places and things usable by everyone: ramps, lifts, Braille signs, audio books, Indian Sign Language.
Avani Lekhara (shooting) has won gold at the Paralympic Games.
traps: Shouting does not help people who are deaf; face them when you speak and learn a few signs.
The problem is access, not the person: ask for a ramp or a ground-floor option.

learn.hook: She can SEW a flower, a farmer can SOW a seed, SO what's the difference? Spelling!
points: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.
sew (to stitch with needle and thread), sow (to plant seeds), so (therefore / very).
there (a place), their (belonging to them), they're (they are).
to (towards), too (also / very much), two (the number 2).
More pairs: hear/here, write/right, knew/new, piece/peace, threw/through, sea/see.

example.q: Think it through: Choose the right words: 'Ila can (sew/sow) a (piece/peace) of cloth with her feet, and (their/there) are many who admire her.'
steps: Stitching cloth → sew.
A part of something → piece.
'There are' (introducing something) → there.

learn.reallife: Spell-check can't always help: 'I red the book' is spelt correctly but wrong! Knowing homophones makes your writing clear.

quiz.q: What are homophones?
options: words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings
quiz.explain: Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning and spelling.
steps: Homophones are about sound and meaning.
They sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.
Example: sew, so, sow.
Answer: words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings
quiz.mistake: Confuses homophones with synonyms or antonyms

quiz.q: Which word means 'to stitch with a needle'?
quiz.explain: To sew is to stitch.
steps: 'Sew', 'so' and 'sow' sound alike.
To stitch with a needle is to sew.
To sow is to plant seeds.
Answer: sew

quiz.q: Fill in: 'They're happy because ___ team won.'
quiz.explain: 'Their' shows the team belongs to them.
steps: The team belongs to them.
'Their' shows belonging.
'There' is a place and 'they're' means 'they are'.
Answer: their

quiz.q: Fill in: 'The tea is ___ hot to drink.'
quiz.explain: 'Too' means 'more than enough' here.
steps: The tea is more hot than you can drink.
'Too' means more than enough.
'To' is a preposition and 'two' is a number.
Answer: too

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Please come ___ and sit beside me.'
quiz.explain: 'Here' means this place.
steps: 'Come ___' needs a word for this place.
'Here' means this place.
'Hear' is what you do with your ears.
Answer: here

quiz.q: Which sentence uses through or threw correctly?
options: The ball went threw the window.
The ball went thorough the window.
The ball went through the window.
The ball went though the window.
quiz.explain: 'Through' means in one side and out of the other. 'Threw' is the past of 'throw'.
steps: The ball went in one side of the window and out the other.
That meaning is 'through'.
'Threw' is the past of 'throw'; 'though' means however.
Answer: The ball went through the window.

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Grandma ___ a lovely shawl for me last winter.'
quiz.explain: Stitching a shawl is sewing; past tense: sewed.
steps: Making a shawl with needle and thread is sewing.
'Last winter' needs the past: sewed.
'Sowed' means planted seeds.
Answer: sewed

quiz.q: Fill in: 'I ___ the answer before the teacher asked.'
quiz.explain: 'Knew' is the past of 'know'; 'new' means not old.
steps: The blank needs the past of 'know'.
know → knew.
'New' means not old; 'knowed' is not a word.
Answer: knew

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'Sew, sow and so sound exactly the same! How do I know which one to write?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Homophones sound the same but have different meanings and spellings. I'll sew my nest, not sow it!
teach.nudge: If they sound the same, what is different about homophones?

revise.summary: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings. Choosing the right one depends on the meaning in the sentence.
focus: Other pairs: hear/here, knew/new, piece/peace, threw/through
remember: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.
sew (to stitch), sow (to plant seeds), so (therefore / very).
there (a place), their (belonging to them), they're (they are).
to (towards), too (also / very much), two (the number 2).
traps: Don't confuse homophones with synonyms or antonyms.
Don't mix up sew (stitch) and sow (plant): 'Grandma sewed a shawl'.
Don't confuse 'threw' (past of 'throw') with 'through' (in one side and out of the other).
